hiddenNotes: Published tuition ranges widely: about 25,000 dollars at public universities (the out-of-state rate international students pay) to 45,000-plus at private ones, so the figure here is a representative midpoint.
US universities require their own health insurance and often auto-enroll you in a plan costing 1,500 to 2,500 dollars a year, on top of any cover you arrange yourself.
There is little need-based aid for international undergraduates, and all-in costs at top private universities can exceed 80,000 dollars a year.

sources.name: US Department of State: student visa fees

hiddenNotes: The Immigration Health Surcharge (about 776 pounds a year) is paid upfront for your whole course before you arrive, on top of the visa fee.
London living costs run well above the rest of the UK: the Home Office sets student maintenance at 1,483 pounds a month for London versus 1,136 elsewhere.
Medicine and dentistry cost far more, up to 38,000 to 70,000 pounds a year for international students.

hiddenNotes: The proof-of-funds requirement more than doubled to CAD 22,895 per year for a single student outside Quebec, far above the roughly CAD 10,000 many families still budget for.
Ontario's UHIP health insurance is mandatory and rises to about CAD 948 for 2026/27, and it excludes dental, prescription drugs, and mental health unless you add supplementary cover.
Tuition here is the national average for international undergraduates; high-demand programs and top universities charge considerably more.

sources.name: IRCC: Proof of funds for a study permit

hiddenNotes: Australia now asks student-visa applicants to show AUD 29,710 a year in living funds, among the highest thresholds anywhere, and the student visa fee jumped to AUD 2,000 (rising again in 2026).
Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) is mandatory for the whole visa, around AUD 500 to 800 a year.
Tuition varies widely by course; medicine and veterinary science run far above the AUD 20,000 to 45,000 band typical for other bachelor’s degrees.

sources.name: Department of Home Affairs: Student visa (subclass 500)

hiddenNotes: Public universities charge no tuition in most states; you pay only a semester contribution of roughly 350 euros, often including a public-transport pass. Baden-Württemberg is the exception, charging non-EU students about 3,000 euros a year.
You must park about 11,904 euros in a blocked account before arrival to prove you can support yourself, released to you monthly.
Public student health insurance runs about 120 euros a month and is mandatory before you can enrol.

sources.name: DAAD: cost of living and studying in Germany
German Missions: blocked account and student visa

hiddenNotes: From mid-2025 you must pay at least 6,000 euros of fees (or the full fee if lower) before the visa is granted, plus show 10,000 euros a year for living costs.
Non-EU students must buy private health insurance (roughly 160 to 600 euros a year); you are not covered by the public system.
Dublin rents are among the steepest in Europe and can dwarf the 10,000-euro official living estimate.

sources.name: Education in Ireland: fees and costs

hiddenNotes: Non-EU bachelor tuition varies a lot by field and institution, from about 6,000 to 15,000 euros; the figure here is a representative midpoint.
If you take a part-time job you must switch to Dutch basic health insurance (about 130 euros a month) instead of cheaper student cover.
Student housing is scarce and Amsterdam rooms can run 650 to 1,200 euros a month, well above the national average.

sources.name: Study.eu: Netherlands tuition and cost of living

hiddenNotes: The MOE Tuition Grant cuts tuition sharply (to about SGD 21,400 a year at NUS) but legally bonds you to work for a Singapore-registered company for three years after graduating.
Without the grant, tuition runs SGD 30,000 to 60,000-plus a year; the grant is the norm but the bond is a real commitment.
Singapore is among the world’s most expensive cities; housing and daily costs are the steepest of the eight.
